case_name: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra
legal_concepts: Culpable Homicide Not Amounting to Murder
judgment_text: The test of 'grave and sudden provocation' is whether a reasonable man, belonging to the same class of society as the accused, placed in the situation in which the accused was placed, would be so provoked as to lose his self-control. The provocation must be grave and sudden to deprive the accused of the power of self-control. Where sufficient time has elapsed between the provocation and the fatal blow for passion to cool down and reason to exert its control, the offence is murder under Section 101/103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly IPC Section 300/302).

case_name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
judgment_text: A real and abiding concern for the dignity of human life postulates resistance to taking a human life through law's instrumentality. That ought not to be done save in the rarest of rare cases when the alternative option is unquestionably foreclosed. For determining whether the death penalty should be awarded for murder under Section 103 of BNS (IPC Section 302), the Court must pay due regard to both the crime and the criminal, balancing aggravating and mitigating circumstances.

case_name: Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab
judgment_text: The death penalty for murder under Section 103 of BNS 2023 may be awarded when the collective conscience of the community is so shocked that it will expect the holders of judicial power to inflict death penalty irrespective of their personal opinion as regards desirability or otherwise of retaining death penalty. Guidelines include: (i) Manner of commission of murder; (ii) Motive for commission of murder; (iii) Anti-social or socially abhorrent nature of the crime; (iv) Magnitude of crime; (v) Personality of victim of murder.

case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh v. Rayavarapu Punnayya
judgment_text: The scheme of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 separates culpable homicide (Section 100) and murder (Section 101/103). All murder is culpable homicide, but not all culpable homicide is murder. Culpable homicide is the genus and murder is the species. Whenever a court is confronted with the question whether the offence is murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder, the court will be required to approach the problem in three stages: (1) whether the accused has done an act which has caused death; (2) whether this act amounts to culpable homicide; (3) whether it falls within any of the clauses of Section 101.

case_name: Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab
legal_concepts: Sufficient in Ordinary Course of Nature to Cause Death
judgment_text: To establish murder under Section 101 Clause Thirdly of BNS 2023 (IPC Section 300 Thirdly), the prosecution must prove four elements: First, it must establish, quite objectively, that a bodily injury is present; Secondly, the nature of the injury must be proved; Thirdly, it must be proved that there was an intention to inflict that particular bodily injury; Fourthly, it must be established that the injury inflicted was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

case_name: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan @ Pappu Yadav
judgment_text: Criminal conspiracy under Section 61 of BNS 2023 consists in the agreement of two or more persons to do an unlawful act or a lawful act by unlawful means. Direct evidence of conspiracy is seldom available; conspiracy must be inferred from the surrounding circumstances, conduct of the accused, and meeting of minds prior to or at the time of the commission of murder under Section 103.

case_name: State of Tamil Nadu v. Nalini
judgment_text: The gist of the offence of criminal conspiracy under Section 61 of BNS 2023 is a bare agreement to commit an offence. It is not necessary that every conspirator must take an active part in the commission of each and every execution of the conspiracy. However, mere knowledge or discussion without agreement does not constitute conspiracy. Once agreement is established, every conspirator is liable for acts done in furtherance of the common conspiracy to commit murder under Section 103.

case_name: Tukaram v. State of Maharashtra
judgment_text: Passive submission under fear or authority does not constitute voluntary consent under Section 63/64 of BNS 2023. The absence of physical injuries on the person of the victim does not necessarily mean that she was a consenting party. The judgment triggered comprehensive statutory reforms in Indian rape law, establishing strict legal standards regarding consent and custodial authority.

case_name: State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh
judgment_text: The testimony of a victim of sexual assault under Section 63/64 of BNS 2023 stands on a higher footing than an accomplice or ordinary witness. Corroboration of the victim's testimony is not an imperative requirement of law but a rule of prudence. Courts must handle sexual assault cases with sensitivity and conduct trials in camera to protect the dignity and privacy of the victim.

case_name: Independent Thought v. Union of India
judgment_text: Sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is protected, but sexual intercourse with a minor wife below eighteen years constitutes rape under Section 63 of BNS 2023. Human rights of a child bride and her right to bodily integrity cannot be compromised on the altar of marital exceptions.

case_name: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
judgment_text: The constitutional validity of criminal defamation under Section 356 of BNS 2023 (formerly IPC Section 499/500) is upheld. Right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is not absolute and is subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2). Right to reputation is an inherent facet of Article 21 Right to Life, and criminal defamation constitutes a reasonable restriction.

case_name: Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar
judgment_text: The provisions of criminal law penalizing acts threatening public order or security of the state must be interpreted so that speech or expression is punished only when there is an incitement to violence or a public disorder. Strong criticism of government measures without incitement to violence does not constitute an offence under criminal law.

case_name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
judgment_text: Freedom of speech and of the press includes freedom of circulation. Restrictions imposed on the dissemination of views cannot be justified unless they directly relate to public order or security of the State, establishing foundational limits against arbitrary state intimidation.

case_name: Pyare Lal Bhargava v. State of Rajasthan
judgment_text: To constitute theft under Section 303 of BNS 2023 (IPC Section 378), it is not necessary that the taking of the property must be permanent. Even a temporary removal of a file or document from the possession of a government office without consent with dishonest intention to show it to an unauthorized person constitutes theft.

case_name: K.N. Mehra v. State of Rajasthan
judgment_text: The essential ingredients of theft under Section 303 of BNS 2023 are: (1) Movable property; (2) In possession of any person; (3) Intention to take dishonestly out of possession; (4) Without consent; (5) Moving in order to such taking. Dishonest intention exists if there is wrongful gain to one or wrongful loss to another, even if temporary.

case_name: State of West Bengal v. Sadhu Khan
legal_concepts: Minimum Number of Persons for Dacoity
judgment_text: Theft becomes robbery under Section 309 of BNS 2023 if, in order to the committing of theft or in committing theft, the offender voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint. When five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit robbery, it constitutes dacoity under Section 310 of BNS 2023.

case_name: Shri Ram v. State of U.P.
judgment_text: To constitute abetment by instigation under Section 45/49 of BNS 2023, there must be active suggestion, encouragement, or incitement by the abettor to do the unlawful act. Mere presence at the scene of crime without any active participation, encouragement, or common intention does not render a person an abettor.

case_name: Jaswantrai Manilal Akhaney v. State of Bombay
judgment_text: To establish criminal breach of trust under Section 316 of BNS 2023, the prosecution must prove that the accused was entrusted with property or with domain over property, and that he dishonestly misappropriated or converted it to his own use in violation of law or legal contract governing such trust.

case_name: State of Gujarat v. Jaswantlal Nathalal
judgment_text: Entrustment is an essential ingredient of criminal breach of trust under Section 316 of BNS 2023. Where property is sold or transferred under a commercial contract, ownership passes to the buyer, and failure to fulfill contract terms does not amount to criminal breach of trust unless entrustment in a fiduciary capacity is established.

case_name: Dr. Vimla v. Delhi Administration
judgment_text: The expression 'fraudulently' involves two elements: deceit and injury to the person deceived. To constitute forgery under Section 335/336 of BNS 2023, there must be a false document made with intent to cause damage or injury, or to support any claim or title, or to cause any person to part with property or enter into a contract.

case_name: Sheila Sebastian v. R. Jawaharaj
judgment_text: A person can be convicted of forgery under Section 335/336 of BNS 2023 only if he himself has made or executed the false document or played an active role in creating it. Impersonation or making of a false document by a third party without proof of creation by the accused cannot sustain a conviction for forgery.

case_name: S.S. Chheena v. Vijay Kumar Mahajan
judgment_text: Abetment involves a mental process of instigating a person or intentionally aiding a person in doing of a thing. Without a positive act on the part of the accused to instigate or aid in committing the offence under Section 45/49 of BNS 2023, conviction for abetment cannot be sustained.

case_name: Virendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
legal_concepts: Apprehension of Death or Grievous Hurt
judgment_text: The right of private defence under Sections 34-41 of BNS 2023 is a preventive and not a punitive right. It is available only to a person who is unlawfully attacked and is subjected to reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt. The force used in exercising private defence must be proportionate to the injury apprehended.

case_name: Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab
legal_concepts: Private Defence of Person and Property
judgment_text: The Supreme Court summarized 11 fundamental principles governing the right of private defence under Sections 34-41 of BNS 2023: (1) Self-preservation is the prime instinct of every human being; (2) Right of private defence is available against unlawful aggression; (3) A person exercising private defence need not run away to avoid attack; (4) Force used must be proportionate; (5) Right extends to protection of person and property.

case_name: Romesh Chandra Arora v. State
judgment_text: To establish criminal intimidation under Section 351 of BNS 2023 (IPC Section 503), the prosecution must prove a threat to cause injury to the person, reputation, or property of another, with intent to cause alarm to that person or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do. Blackmail through threats to publish defamatory photographs constitutes criminal intimidation.
